utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, there is just three small matters, one that is extremely important and may I deal with that at the start? Can I on behalf of all the lawyers present congratulate you on your elevation to vice-president, and I suppose it's being slightly flippant by saying they almost got it right but we utter our congratulations to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, and all counsel and all present, thank you so very much. It was a great honour that was bestowed on me by the Judges this morning, an extra load perhaps that I carry with good heart, good cheer and good energy. And I would add that also welcome today is a permanent Judge rather than as an ad litem judge was Judge Van den Wyngaert. So you have two new lots of life on the Bench as from now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Pleasure. May I move on to two smaller matters? One that relates to the transcript that was used yesterday for the meeting between Cyrus Vance and Mr. Sljivancanin et al. That was not made an exhibit, and I wonder perhaps if that could be made an exhibit, although I know there may be a small issue in relation to translation in two small parts. But nevertheless, I will make an application for it to be an exhibit in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which tab was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It wasn't on a tab. It was the separate -- it was the separate sheet held together by a staple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's got the number, the last four numbers, 7244.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. I don't mind having this video footage admitted into evidence. I spoke to Mr. Moore just now and expressed my bewilderment that we didn't do this yesterday. What I have a problem with is the transcript that we had in our hands, the hard copy. There is a portion missing in the B/C/S version, and there is something in English that I couldn't find in the B/C/S version. Therefore, I would like to have this retranslated by the CLSS, and in the meantime, can we just mark it for identification? That's all I had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I was told about small concerns and I, of course, will have that looked at again, and we have isolated the two areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will for the time being be marked for identification, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked with number 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then the video itself, I suspect, should be a separate item, in any event, and that is -- it's an excerpt, number 327, and it's V00/1231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be exhibit number 70, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ambassador. I'm sorry in the handling of all of those matters you've been rather overlooked. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the commencement of your evidence which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tapuskovic? Cross-examined by Ms. Tapuskovic:

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Okun. My name is Mira Tapuskovic. I'm one of the attorneys of Miroslav Radic. As we were preparing for your testimony, we from the Defence team received very little information on you. The Prosecution only disclosed to us four pages of your diary in -- with translations, and now we had occasion to see that these diaries of yours are quite voluminous. You were introduced to the Defence and to the Trial Chamber as an international witness. That means that you were to tell us about the general context of events taking place in Croatia in the second half of 1991. Yesterday, several times, you mentioned various names of officials, officers you met in the course of your mission in the former Yugoslavia, and it seemed to me that you yourself speak one of the languages that we refer to here at the Tribunal as B/C/S, meaning Bosnian/Croatian/Serbian. Do you understand any of those languages?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I speak Russian. I read Cyrillic easily, and via Russian, I can understand some Serbo-Croatian, what you call B/C/S. I would not claim to be fluent in Serbo-Croatian, what you call B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it would be interesting to tell to the Trial Chamber that before coming here you testified here twice in two other cases. In 2003, you testified in the case Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was February 2003.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other case where you also appeared as a witness was the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik in 2004; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I testified in that case in June 2004.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In both of these cases, your testimony was quite extensive, lasted several days?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the Krajisnik case, you spoke only about the events which took place in Bosnia following the eruption of the conflict in 1992. Did you at one point in time give evidence about the events in Croatia and what took place in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically. It might well be the case, because the conflict in Yugoslavia was a continuing, almost continuing conflict, and the situation overlapped from republic to republic. So while I can't recall anything specific, there probably was some mention of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will then, when the time comes, refer you back to what you stated then. In addition to the transcripts of your testimony in these two cases, we also received from the Prosecution a brief statement which seems somewhat unusual to us in its form. It is called a declaration. You signed it in 2001. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You signed this declaration on the 14th of August, 2001, and it seems that it was sent to the Prosecution either by fax or by mail, and it pertained solely to Slobodan Milosevic. I'm just now trying to refresh your memory. It's a very short declaration that discussed his ability to control the events in the former Yugoslavia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I was extensively questioned during the Milosevic trial on that point. I'd be grateful if you could make available to me, and perhaps to the Court, this declaration of 2001, which I don't recall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please assist me? Your Honours, I'm now giving to the usher the English version of the declaration signed by the witness in the United States. Could this be put on the ELMO after the witness has taken a look, so that everybody else can see it as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Once the witness has had a chance to look at it, he will no doubt be able to tell us whether he recalls making the statement or affirmation, and if he does, we will proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've read this declaration, Mrs. Tapuskovic. Yes, I do recall it, and I may say it is accurate. Everything in the statement is accurate. I stand by it fully. Indeed I was questioned about it for -- by Mr. Milosevic for numerous hours during the Milosevic trial on these points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Perhaps the document might be put on to the machine next to you where you will be able to see it but it will also be able to come up on our screens. If it can be turned so that the ambassador can read it, please. Thank you. Yes, Mrs. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all I wanted was to put this to the witness so that he can either confirm or deny signing such a declaration. The witness first said that he did not remember signing this and only upon seeing the declaration he accepted it as his own, and I have no further questions concerning the declaration. Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you want it tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no need, Your Honours for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us about various conferences. In fact, you mentioned two conferences on the former Yugoslavia. One of them, as far as I was able to understand, was called the conference on Yugoslavia; and the second one was called the conference on the former Yugoslavia. Did I understand this well?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have the first title correct. The second title was not quite correct. The first title, the first conference, was called the Conference on Yugoslavia. That was the EC-sponsored conference we've discussed, which lasted from August 1991 -- yes, August 1991 until August 1992, and that was the one that, as we discussed, had the responsibility for the comprehensive solution of the Yugoslav problem. The next conference, the second one, was the International Conference on the former Yugoslavia, which actually convened primarily in Geneva, and it existed from September 1992 until approximately 1995. I was the deputy co-chairman of that conference, the international conference, from September 1992 until May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your earlier testimonies in the other two trials, you told us that the task that you were given on the 25th of September, 1991 in the resolution was to establish peace in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Yesterday you also mentioned something interesting, namely, that you were a member of a fact-finding mission. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is standard diplomatic procedure when you form a mission and you go to a country, particularly where there is conflict. The first thing you have to do is, before you can even begin to mediate between the parties, the first thing, of course, that one has to do is to seek to establish the factual situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 of the Security Council Resolution sets forth legal framework for your mission. Paragraph 3 specifies that the United Nations, without any undue delay, offering assistance and advice to the government of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. Do you remember this paragraph 3 of the resolution?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I have it in front of me. Yes, I'm looking at it, and you've characterised it partially correctly and partially incorrectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, other provisions of that resolution, did they urge the parties to abide by the cease-fire agreement of the 17th and 22nd September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Article 4 of resolution 713, I quote: "Strongly urges all parties to abide strictly by the cease-fire agreements of 17 September 1991 and 22 September 1991."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you, Mr. Okun, were in charge of fact-finding, please tell us whether the parties to the conflict complied with these instructions of the UN?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no, none of the parties complied with the cease-fires that were unilaterally declared and sometimes not unilaterally by the European Community. There were more than a dozen cease-fires declared by the European Community between July 1991 and December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber whether the resolution also introduced weapons embargo or, rather, an embargo on delivery of arms and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chapter 6 reads, and I quote: "Decides under Chapter 7 of the Charter of the United Nations that all states shall, for the purposes of establishing peace and stability in Yugoslavia, immediately implement a general and complete embargo on all deliveries of weapons and military equipment to Yugoslavia until the Security Council decides otherwise following consultation between the Secretary-General and the government of Yugoslavia." That's paragraph 6, operative paragraph 6, of Resolution 713.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun. When you testify in the Krajisnik case in 2004, as you spoke about the other international conference on the former Yugoslavia, because in the meantime certain republics had been recognised, you said that the seat of that conference moved from Geneva to New York. If you don't remember saying that -- first of all let me ask you, do you remember that, that that is how it was?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The conference seat moved from Geneva to New York in February 1993. Excuse me, I should add that we didn't simply move to the city of New York. We moved specifically to UN headquarters in New York city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a very important explanation that you just provided, Mr. Okun. I would like to ask the usher to assist me, if possible, and put a page of the transcript from the Krajisnik case on the ELMO, as you have told us that you don't remember all of the details that you had mentioned of the occasion. Thank you. Your Honours, in order to proceed faster, I will give two copies to the usher. They are identical. One is intended for the witness and the other one is for the ELMO. The same sentence has been underlined in both copies. Thank you. Mr. Okun, can you confirm that the copy that I have just provided, the copy that you have in front of you, is identical to the copy that the usher has placed on the ELMO? This is something we need to do for the sake of the transcript. So if you could please check to your right, look at the ELMO, and see the document there is identical to the one that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are identical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure if everybody can see this on their screens. The words that are highlighted in yellow, sir, could you please read them out? It's only two lines.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your permission, may I read the entire answer? It adds only one line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. Just the highlighted portion, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you're telling me I cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mrs. Tapuskovic. There is one answer. I think it would be more important that the whole answer be read than just a sentence from it. If you would, thank you, ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, certainly.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The preceding question, very briefly, was: "Let me ask you," I'm quoting, "more generally whether the discussions continued among the parties and the representatives of the international conference on former Yugoslavia, and my" -- to go to -- the question continues. My answer was, and I quote: "Yes, after the presentation, of course, there were" -- the presentation here refers to the Vance Owen peace plan which had been presented to the parties to the conflict several weeks previously in January 1993. Excuse me. "After the presentation, of course, there were acceptances and rejections and the plan was complex in certain respects. The conference moved in February to New York to be closer to the United Nations and to decision-makers in Washington."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun. What I would like to ask you in relation to the last words you have just spoken, from this answer that at the time you provided in the Krajisnik case, can you please tell us who are these decision-makers in Washington, since you seem to be using the plural here? Are we talking about the US government? Are we talking about the president? Or are we talking about the institution that sent you away on a peace mission to Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to preface my answer with a small introduction as to this answer, which is very simple and straightforward, and I will proceed to answer it again. The conference, as I've mentioned, was a combined conference of the EC and the United Nations. In my capacity and Mr. Vance's, we were the United Nations side. Lord Owen was the co-chairman for the EC. Now, since the United States was -- is not a member of the EC, and there are -- were then about 140 or so members of the United Nations, and although, of course, it is a fact that Mr. Vance and I are American citizens, our capacity was in -- we were there as UN people, wearing blue hats, so to speak, and it was the consensus view of all of the parties to the conference, including all of the Yugoslav parties, that we could move more quickly and that we could facilitate our discussions if we were in New York at the headquarters and were in the same time zone as the principal players. Now, I say the United States was not represented at this conference, and it is, I think, fair to say that the United States of America is an important member of the world community, and it was common sense to have our members consult, as we did with other countries constantly. If you look through my diaries, which you have, you will see us in Italy, consulting with the Italian foreign minister, in Germany with the German foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must interrupt you. I fully agree with you as far as the consulting part is concerned. It is logical for you to consult a number of countries, but you said here that you had to be in the vicinity of the decision-makers. My question was brief and clear: The United States, at the time, for you, sir, were they the decision-makers as concerned events occurring in Europe? Because you transferred the seat of the conference from Europe to the United States at the exact point in time when the war began to flare up, as it were. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Now I understand your question. Decision-makers in Washington means they are decision-makers in Washington, clearly not decision-makers in Europe. That's I think self-evident. They have the Secretary of State, for example, people like that, they -- the kind of people who make decisions for their government. They don't make decisions for other governments. And they did not make decisions for Mr. Vance or me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you received your mandate on the 25th of September, 1991, did you not? Your first visit, as you told us yesterday, or rather, as my colleague Mr. Moore elicited from you in chief, was on the 12th of October. Can you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But let me clarify. It is not correct to say we received our mandate, Mr. Vance and me -- and I. It is not correct to say that we received it on September 25th. On September 25th, the Secretary-General received a mandate from the Security Council. We received our mandate on or about October 8th or 9th, when Mr. Vance was called and asked to take on the job and I was called to take on the job. So it was really about October 8 or 9 that we received our mandate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. This means that your preparation time for that mission, an important mission to all the citizens of Yugoslavia and the entire community alike was briefer, shorter than I believed. All you had was a couple of days before you arrived in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vance had, in 1991, about 45 years or so diplomatic experience at every level, the Sinai conflict, the conflict in Cyprus. I had about 30 years diplomatic experience in conflict solution and management. Neither of us was unaware of what was going on in Yugoslavia at the time. And, of course, we went there as we've all agreed again in standard diplomatic practice on a fact-finding mission to find out for ourselves and make our own independent judgements as to what was going on and report back to the Secretary-General and the Security Council. All of this is quite normal. Excuse me, could I ask the Registrar to have on the screen your questions, our dialogue? I thank you. It's come back already. Thank you. Sorry to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Mr. Okun. You can then confirm that you and Mr. Vance were already sufficiently familiar with the situation in the former Yugoslavia before your first mission and your first physical arrival, as it were, on this mission, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were familiar in a general way. Lord Carrington, for example, flew to New York immediately after we were appointed, to brief us extensively on the work of the community. Of course, he was the principal negotiator, so there was no better person than he, and we spent hours, if not days, with him. We also had the peacekeeping people and the political people of the United Nations secretariat made available to us. They were extremely cooperative. So in the interim, between our appointment and our departure, we were not painting our finger-nails.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you so much. In preparation for your testimony, as I said at the outset, we had little material at our disposal. However, having familiarised ourselves with the answers that you provided yesterday, quite aside from any touristic reasons that you may have had in 1997 and some other possible visits, as far as this mission is concerned, the one that has to do with this indictment, you were in the former Yugoslavia a total of three times, and if we use simple mathematics, it seems that you spent a total of 20 days in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Sir, do you believe that a 20-day period would be sufficient for you to fully familiarise yourself with the situation as it was on the ground in an area where the war was gaining force, as it were?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we had enough time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you submit a special report after each and every one of your visits to the Secretary-General, or did you only submit one report late in 1991 or at a different time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We submitted reports to the security Council through the Secretary-General at the end of each mission. The first report was in October 1991. It's lengthy. It had several annexes. I couldn't repeat it for you verbatim. It's been 14 years. And it is probably 40 or 50 pages long. But it was a very detailed report, and we did that and that's one of the reasons I kept my diary notes was precisely so that we would be accurate in reporting to the Security Council what we found. I commend you to read those reports, if --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you haven't read them, I will refer to them probably several times today because they are all public documents and they gave Mr. Vance and the Secretary-General's and my view officially to the Security Council. They were all available at the time and are all available today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point in time, all I wanted to know about was the technical aspect, more specifically, how many reports you submitted and when, following your visits to the former Yugoslavia. It would seem that throughout this entire mission, you had very good relations with both the UNHCR and the International Red Cross. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had good relations with all parties, with all parties, the fighting parties and the humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These humanitarian organisations, UNHCR, the International Red Cross, the ECMM, did they brief you or submit any special reports to you that were later incorporated in your own report?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall receiving anything in writing from any of the organisations you mention, and incidentally the name of the committee is the International Committee of the Red Cross. Please correct the record on that. But we received extensive oral comments from them about the situation. Of course, that was natural, part of our job to learn, as you've correctly pointed out, it was important to inform ourselves as fully as possible of the situation on the ground, and there is no dispute about that. So it was quite natural that one would speak to the humanitarian organisations, to the representatives of the European Community, the monitoring group, the ECMM, the monitors, although I would not call them a humanitarian organisation. They were monitors. They were observers of the situation. But that was quite natural, and we did speak to them. But to answer your question, I don't recall ever receiving a -- anything in writing, although it's possible. We may have -- they may have shown us reports they made back to their headquarters. That's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that there were several disagreements between the ECMM and the International Red Cross regarding what was happening in Croatia in the autumn of 1991? Please, yes or no, if possible.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were disagreements between almost all of the parties as to what was happening in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Throughout 1991, did you meet your colleague, Mr. Zimmerman at any time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many times specifically in 1991?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have that specifically in my memory. It was probably three or four times, something like that. The gentleman that Ms. Tapuskovic is referring to is Warren Zimmerman who was then the American ambassador in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification, Mr. Okun. If I may, I would now like to go back to what happened in Croatia. This is not necessarily about how the international community viewed it, but from the point of view of how people in Yugoslavia perceived this, what do you think could have been defined as the one turning point, the watershed, of what was going on at the time in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is a question --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Croatia, yes. It's an interesting question. It's one, of course, for the historians to answer, and it is probably controversial to this day as to what people -- as to how the international community -- let me answer that in two parts. You said international community and the people of Yugoslavia. As to the international community, that answer is somewhat easier because, as I mentioned yesterday, and no need to did go into detail in it, everybody was aware of the offer, the treaty basically that Lord Carrington put down on October 18, 1991, the arrangements for a general settlement. Everybody knew that five republics had accepted it, that only Serbia rejected it. That was a major point. There were of course differences within the international community on that, particularly differences on the question of recognition of Slovenia and Croatia. As far as the people of Yugoslavia are concerned, I wouldn't claim to speak for them. I don't know who can claim to speak for them. But I think it probably fair to say that it depended on which people, which "narod" you were asking. We saw the leaders, we spoke to a lot of people. In Macedonia, for example, President Gligorov and others down the line were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in order to be brief, Mr. Okun, does the term, the log revolution or timber revolution or "balvan revolucija" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The timber revolution?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They used to call it the log revolution.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I'm not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you're not aware of the term, there is no need to go any further into that. This is something that happened in August 1990 --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1? When did it occur?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: August 1990, when the Croatian special police attacked a police station in a Serbian settlement in Croatia but we can just move on. In May 1990, Franjo Tudjman was elected president. Yesterday, we touched on a lot of constitutional issues. I don't think there is any need to go into those now. However, there is something I would like to ask you regarding the declaration of independence of Croatia. Do you perhaps remember the date when Croatia of its own accord declared independence?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain. I believe it was June 25, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct. That's correct, Mr. Okun. Do you agree that the European Community made recommendations to the other European countries to prevent a premature recognition of Croatia or any other republics of the former Yugoslavia? Is this something that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite familiar with that subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the UN Secretary-General, in December, advised the Dutch foreign minister to refrain from prematurely recognising Croatia as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm fully aware of the Secretary-General's letter, which concerned not only Croatia but Slovenia. He recommended --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just talking about Croatia now, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But one can't talk about these things in isolation, Madam. There was a continuum. It would be taking matters out of context not to look at the overall situation - excuse me - but that must be taken in order to give the full picture to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun. As I continue my cross-examination, I will make an effort to adopt a broader view, but we mustn't go too far from the point. We mustn't stray too far from the point. In your testimony in the Milosevic and Krajisnik trials, you spoke about the general context. You spoke about how things were in the former Yugoslavia. Here, on the other hand, we will have to focus on a much smaller picture, both in terms of the territory covered and in terms of time. Now back to this recommendation to refrain from a premature recognition. Do you think this was because at the time there, there were integration processes afoot in Europe and this development was believed to have a possible negative effect on the treaty of Maastricht?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the case at hand. The situation was as follows, if I may explain it to you. Both Slovenia and Croatia, in this case, let's stick with Croatia, I agree with you on trying to keep focused, along with Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia, had all requested recognition by the EC. In answer to that request, the European Community, and Lord Carrington in particular, asked the Badinter Commission, the commission of arbitration, to issue a decision as to which of the four countries merited recognition. The Badinter Commission so decided in December, and their tentative decision was that Slovenia and Macedonia merited recognition, that Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia did not. The reason they gave -- excuse me, Madam I must not be interrupted on this point. You asked the question. I'm trying to explain to the Court the situation. If you want to explain the situation do so, but you asked me to explain it. To continue: The reason they gave for not approving the request for recognition of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were in the case of Croatia, they said they needed to pass some legislation protecting the rights of minorities, which Croatia did. In the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Badinter Commission decided that only an expression of the will of the people would make it acceptable. So in those two cases, they temporised with the recognition. And therefore, the letter about which you have asked me, the letter from the Secretary-General to Hans Van den Broek, the Dutch foreign minister, was consistent with that recommendation. It was also the very strong recommendation of Mr. Vance and myself against early, selective, premature, chaotic recognition policy. Have I answered the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. However, regardless of these conclusions reached by the Badinter Commission, and the first one was reached in November, as far as I recollect, and regardless of the letter that the UN Secretary-General sent to the Dutch foreign minister, at one point in time, Germany made a unilateral decision to grant recognition to Croatia, did it not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The German government, following a vote in its parliament, they were instructed to do so. So they recognised Croatia and Slovenia about two weeks, 14 or 15 days, earlier than the European Community. The German recognition came about Christmas time 1991, and the entire recognition of Croatia and Slovenia by the EC was January 15th, 1992. So they were pretty close in time, although they weren't simultaneous.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters for interrupting them. You said quite well that perhaps the date of German recognition of Croatia is not so important, even though, as a sign of their gratitude, Croats built a monument to Genscher and sang a song thanking Germany. However, do you think that it was -- somehow it was wrong for them to recognise Croatia, despite the contrary recommendation given by the Badinter Commission?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, it was my view, Mr. Vance's view, that of the Secretary-General, that it would have been the wiser policy for the EC to maintain a united front and recognise all the Yugoslav republics that desired independence, as you know there were four republics, not just one or two, there were four, we felt that a coordinated recognition policy was wiser than a selective premature policy of recognition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would suggest that we take a break, in accordance with our yesterday's agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I was hanging on in case you needed to ask more questions on that topic. That was all. We will break now and resume at quarter minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic? Oh, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague, Lukic, would like to bring up a procedural issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. First of all, I'd like to clarify something concerning our schedule for tomorrow. We have received information that there is a likelihood that we would be working tomorrow in the morning. On behalf of all Defence teams, I can say that we will put in additional effort to prepare in full our cross-examination of the next witness, who is coming here pursuant to Rule 92 bis so that the Trial Chamber and all parties could complete their work tomorrow somewhat earlier, now that it has become possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. We heard this morning that the trial listed this morning -- tomorrow morning has had to be adjourned so that the courtroom will be available. It occurred to the Chamber that it might be good for everybody if we commenced sitting tomorrow at, say, 10.00 in the morning and finished earlier in the afternoon than possible. In other words, returning to something like normal court hours, rather than the early morning, late afternoon shifts that we operate in at the moment. It's helpful to learn that it will be practical from the Defence point of view to think of doing that. I will check with Mr. Moore and if it is, we will make such a change. Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There are no difficulties, apparent difficulties, to the Prosecution for a change of time. We'll accommodate my learned friends and the Court in any way that we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber then will sit tomorrow in the morning and afternoon but commence sitting at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before I put my next question to the witness, I would like to ask for your guidance concerning this transcript from the Krajisnik case. Is it a typical procedure to tender into evidence transcript from another case? And if so, is it acceptable for this Trial Chamber? In which case I would like to have this page, 449, of the transcript be tendered into evidence. I am asking for your instructions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer has to be very much like many of the answers that you've had from the ambassador. I have to give an explanation. The first is that it depends very much upon what it is you're seeking to tender and for what purpose. If you wanted the whole of the transcript of a witness to become evidence in this case, that would require a special motion. It would have to be considered by the other side, and they might want that witness to attend for cross-examination. Now I realise that's not what you are proposing, but I thought I might explain it to you in case something like that should arise in future and you would then understand how to approach it. If it is the case that you simply want an answer or a passage or two from an extensive transcript, recorded as evidence in the transcript so that it is seen that this is what the particular witness said on another occasion, it's not normal to receive the transcript as an exhibit, merely that when you ask the questions, as you have done here, what was said on the last occasion is read so that it appears in the transcript of this trial. Now, if it's the page that you put to the witness earlier, the transcript records now fully the question and the answer so that it is now clearly in evidence in this trial that this witness gave that evidence earlier, and he has explained that that is his -- the correct position and so forth. So you really don't need now to tender anything further.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the explanation, Your Honours. This will be beneficial to all of us in our future case in this trial, as we will have many witnesses who testified in other cases. Therefore, this explanation of yours is of great assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, we can proceed with questions. I will now go back to the issue of the recognition of Croatia as an independent state, because this is one of the very important matters in trying to describe the full picture of the situation as it existed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, which is precisely the subject of your testimony here. You have mentioned Badinter Commission to us several times, or the arbitration commission, as it is otherwise known. Will you tell me this, please: Were the decisions of this commission mandatory to the then republics of the former Yugoslavia or to the entire Yugoslavia at the time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My best recollection is that the decisions of the arbitration commission, which was its official name, unofficially people called it the Badinter Commission, both names, of course, mean the commission that I talked about, we are discussing, I believe their judgements were advisory in nature, but that's a judgement on my part. We were not -- Mr. Vance and I, we were servants of the United Nations and were not bound at all by the Badinter Commissions, although we met on several occasions with Minister Badinter personally. We found those meetings very useful. He's a man of deep humanity and high intelligence and very knowledgeable on the legal issues and so he informed us, informally, of his views. As I said, we consulted as widely as possible in order to get the fullest possible picture about the situation. But it was always a matter of advice, and we were -- and others, orbit, the UN orbit. I believe the decisions as far as the EC were concerned were advisory opinions but I'm not certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Could I respectfully interrupt for one moment? We have had a lot of questions in relation to the constitutional position and opinions expressed by the arbitration commission, whether it is advisory or indeed other matters. The trial content relates specifically, and I accept it may be a narrow interpretation, to what I will call to military control command structure and the killing of over 260 people at Ovcara. For my part, I fail to see the relevance of going into these matters in detail. I certainly have not seen within the Defence briefs any suggestion that what was done would be legitimised in any way by a change in a constitutional position. I don't know if my learned friend would be able to help the Court or myself in relation to that, but we seem to be going around in circles with regard to the political position as it existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I believe the Chamber can save Ms. Tapuskovic any trouble of submission. There can be little doubt that the narrow picture of relevance to this case is as you put. There can also be little doubt that at least from the view-point of those who were members of the then Yugoslav armed forces, that there is a view held, rightly or wrongly, about the legal legitimacy of their position. I think that the Defence must have an opportunity to advance that view, and then, of course, they will be required in their submissions to deal with the legal relevance of that view to the questions of criminal responsibility that arise in this case. But I don't think we can assume that there can be no possible substance in that at this point so as to deny a reasonable exploration of the issue. So we wouldn't interrupt the course of cross-examination on that basis, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't explain it fully. I, of course, understand because of the way the case was put by Mr. Vasic yesterday that there may well be a view that I'll use the general term, the JNA operated believing that they had a legitimate and valid and constitutional basis for intervention at Vukovar/Croatia. I understand that entirely. But we are now into the realms of the arbitration committee, who basically merely make recommendations, and in our submission, while one is extremely interested in much of the evidence that is being given, nevertheless, we would submit that it is now becoming extremely broad by way of cross-examination, and it is difficult to exactly understand the purpose of the cross-examination as it now exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, very briefly, the legal status of Croatia at the time relevant to these events is, as I understand it, an issue that is relevant to the charge in the way I've explained. The evidence of the ambassador, the work of the European Commission and the United Nations, the recognitions given, if any, by other nations, all have a relevance to the position of Croatia, either still as a member of the federation or as an independent state in the world, or in some process of transition. Those matters may legitimately be explored.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Of course, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That doesn't mean that the Chamber would see that we should absorb days and days and days of this case on those issues. Let me make that clear. But the Chamber certainly feels that there is, in this area, some matters that genuinely warrant exploration by the Defence, and we certainly don't propose to interrupt that so long as the matter is dealt with with the proper appreciation of time in the overall context of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for the explanation, Your Honour. In the introductory part of my cross-examination today, I specified precisely that, namely, that this witness was introduced to the Chamber and to us as an international witness testifying about the general context of events which are relevant for this case. And based on those reasons, I proceeded putting questions either about the Badinter Commission or other issues. My further examination will not be very long. I just have a few more questions about this, to complete the picture precisely of those matters that you have mentioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, do you remember that immediately before the recognition of Croatia as an independent state by Germany first and then European Community, foreign minister or foreign ministers of the European Community passed a declaration on the guidelines of the recognition of the new states in Eastern Europe and in the Soviet Union, and another declaration on Yugoslavia? Do you remember those declarations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, but, of course, I'm aware that the former Soviet Union dissolved also in December 1991, simultaneously, almost, with the events that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it refresh your memory if I were to tell you that the conclusion of that declaration of the EC foreign ministers was that the political reality, both in Eastern Europe and in the former Soviet Union, had to be accepted, including the political reality in the territory of the former Yugoslavia? Does that serve that purpose, to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, the Badinter Commission had already judged Yugoslavia to be undergoing a process of dissolution so that this was the factual situation that there was no state anymore. It was in the process of dissolution. That was the understanding, I think, by all parties, based on the arbitration commission's opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the fact that in mid-1991 the situation in Croatia was such that Croatian authorities did not have control over one-third of their territory?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be the case. I would not contest it. I can't confirm it. I didn't -- I wasn't involved. I wasn't there at the time to check on it, so that that may or may not be the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, as a person with a long established career in diplomacy, do you know the standards of the international law and especially international public law about what conditions each subject has to meet in order to be internationally recognised as an independent state? There are three or four standards that have to be fulfilled. Are you familiar with them?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm generally familiar with them. And they, of course, are based in each case on the political reality. They are general guidelines. Each case is decided individually on its merits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, are you familiar with the fact that this criteria are stable population, defined territory, and government which has effective control over the territory and is able to establish relations with other states?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, these are general propositions which have to be interpreted and are interpreted, used by the nations in their recognition policy. Just to give you two very brief examples. When the state of Israel declared its independence in May 1948, it controlled zero per cent of its territory. The Jews controlled nothing because the territory at that time was a British mandate, and it was supposed to go to a partition state between Israel and Palestine, and as we know, Israel was -- Palestine was invaded by the armies of the neighbouring Arab states. Israel declared independence, and within 24 hours, 48 at the latest, both the Soviet Union and the United States recognised Israel and it was promptly admitted into the United Nations, even though it controlled zero per cent of its territory, and it certainly did not have a stable population because there was great fighting and confusion between Palestinian and the Jews. The same obtained in the case of East Timor. There are many, many cases. I don't want to take the time of the Court. But these simply illustrate that the general propositions that you have cited are applied always in individual cases based on the particular reality of the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Okun, but that is precisely why, in the Middle East, the war is still in progress. They haven't resolved the issue of territory. But does that mean that in the case -- in the example that you just gave us, as well as in the case of the former Yugoslavia, they did not uphold the principle u ti possidetis, meaning that you have to control the territory and that it has to be one of the criteria related to the effective control of the territory, which can lead to the proclamation of independence?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to recall for you, Madam, what I said earlier, that each case is divided -- is decided, excuse me, is decided, on an individual case, and to bring it closer to the Yugoslav reality may I remind you that in November 1943, the AVNOJ, Marshal Tito, declared a fight for independence by the partisans supported by the western community. He was given aid and assistance, and at that time, as we know, the German and Italian occupiers occupied all of Yugoslavia except where the partisans and the Chetniks were fighting them. So that I can only reiterate for the benefit of the Court the fact that recognition is always based on the individual merits of the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun. Will you please tell me something about the UN resolution that you mentioned, namely, Resolution 317 [as interpreted] of September 1990? This resolution introduced the embargo on the weapons delivery.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Resolution 713, not 317. I think the letters were simply transposed; it's 713. It's a simple transposition but no problem. Included in that was a general arms embargo. The arms embargo was maintained during most of the fighting for the next several years. It was frequently broken by the parties. Everybody knew that. There was no secret. The sides were busy arming themselves, all of them. It has to also be said that that the embargo came under increasing criticism, particularly when the fighting spread to Bosnia and Herzegovina because the JNA didn't need the weapons, it already had the weapons of an army, and the Bosnian Muslim forces in particular were being prevented from defending themselves. That's a separate issue. But you should be aware that the embargo was formally maintained for two or three more years, and as I say, it became -- it came under increasing criticism by most members of the international community. It was not so much of an issue during the fighting in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the federal government, or rather, the Presidency of the SFRY, in January of 1991, passed a decision on the sale [as interpreted] of illegally admitted weapons and on dissolution of all illegally formed forces?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was aware in a general way that the -- that Belgrade opposed the -- this sort of behaviour. So I don't find it inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the Spegelj affair in January 1991?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, which affair?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Spegelj affair.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid it's not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a scandal involving illegal import of weapons into Croatia. Now we will turn again to something that you mentioned several times yesterday concerning the barracks that were blocked in Croatia. I apologise, Mr. Okun, for the sake of the transcript, page 32, line 6, there is a word "sale" but instead of that word there should be "surrender." Mr. Okun, to continue, based on several pages of your diary, five or six pages that we received, we could see that in several places the issue of unblocking the barracks is mentioned. At the time, you were quite aware of the problem that had been going on for several months already.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I mentioned yesterday, the unblocking of the blockaded JNA barracks was uppermost in General Kadijevic's mind. It was his principal concern expressed to me and to Mr. Vance, and based on that, we undertook strenuous efforts to secure the unblocking of the JNA barracks in Croatia as we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that you signed any agreement to lift the blockade of barracks in the territory of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed this yesterday. There was more than one agreement actually. The major agreement was the Geneva Accord of November 23, 1991, where Mr. Vance and I brought General Kadijevic and Tudjman and Milosevic to Geneva. I mentioned the four points that were in the accord yesterday. The second point was the unblocking of the barracks. We signed another formal agreement, that is to say, the warring parties signed another formal agreement, on December 9th in Zagreb, concerning unblocking and withdrawal of JNA troops and turning over certain equipments, that sort of thing. That was done under my direction. I convened the parties in Zagreb and that was the December 9th agreement. And the third and definitive agreement was the implementing accord of January 2, 1992, signed in Sarajevo, and it implemented the November 23 Geneva Accord. That's why it's called the implementing accord. And with that, the large-scale fighting in Croatia ended. And one month later, the -- to be more specific, six weeks later, the United Nations Security Council passed Resolution 743, which established the peacekeeping force for Croatia, the first time there had ever been a peacekeeping force in Europe. Those were the three principal documents concerning the unblocking of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun. I may have been somewhat imprecise in phrasing the question. But you managed to answer one of my other questions. My question was: Did you sign, with the warring parties, any agreement concerning the unblocking of the barracks? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean did Mr. Vance or I personally sign an agreement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you personally.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I signed as a witness, since I convened the December 9, 1991 meeting between the Croatian and the Serb side. It's quite possible that I might have signed it as a witness, since I was the chairman of the meeting, and, of course, as we have mentioned previously, Mr. Vance signed the Geneva Accord of November 23.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Yesterday you said that you met General Raseta. Do you perhaps remember that you were one of the signatories, even if merely in your capacity as an observer or witness to these negotiations and agreement, to an agreement in December 1991 to unblock a barracks in Dugo Selo?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned yesterday, I spent a good deal of time, perhaps even most of the period from the end of November until the signature of the implementing accord on January 2, 1992, working on unblocking the barracks. So while I have no specific recollection of the barracks in Dugo Selo, it is quite possible because I visited, oh, probably a dozen or so, maybe more, blockaded barracks along the Adriatic coast, and other places as well. So that is quite possible, although, as I say, after having visited so many barracks, it's not always easy to remember exactly. Do you have the document? And if so, could I see it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. This is quite sufficient. Should it be necessary, the Defence will use the help of other witnesses to introduce these documents. You've said quite enough. I understand you do not rule out the possibility that such an agreement was signed or, rather, that you confirmed the signing of such an agreement with your signature.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I confirmed the fact that it might have been possible. I think I said I wasn't -- I said I have no specific recollection --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- for signing -- about the barracks in Dugo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I accept the inference you draw from it. But in the absence of the document itself, and in the absence of a clear recollection of Dugo Selo, I can only say what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: With the utmost respect, if there is going to be a topic pursued in relation to whether a witness has signed a document, he should have an opportunity of knowing whether in actual fact the signature that is suggested to be his is his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. I think that's clear to all parties. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I have already stated, now that the witness has told us that he cannot remember whether he in fact signed such an agreement or not, I will no longer pursue this matter. I don't have the document itself. I have information to this effect. I am merely checking this information pursuant to instructions that I received from my client.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday and on another day recorded in your diary you mentioned something about the clearing of mines. Can you tell us why this problem of mines very often seemed to be linked to the problem of a barracks being blocked?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the JNA officers and soldiers in the barracks told us, more than once, that the area around the barracks had been mined by the Croatians to prevent them from leaving. We, of course, could not check that without being blown up. So we heard them and, of course, I recorded it in my diary. It may have been the case. It may not. Of course, as you will well aware, the Croatians had very few weapons at this time, and so they were seeking to maximise their position by the utilisation of whatever means they had. Now, the question of mines also arose in Vukovar when we were told by Major Sljivancanin that the little bridge across the tiny river could not be crossed by Mr. Vance and me because it was mined, and I've already testified to the fact that we knew that was a falsehood because we could see motor vehicles and pedestrians walking on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yesterday you said you knew General Tus, or rather that you met him. Do you remember this meeting that you had with General Tus?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is recorded in my diary in -- accurately. I don't have it specifically in my head at the moment, but I did meet him on several occasions and they are all recorded in my diary notes, which are available to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The Defence teams were only given a single page of your diary. The first name we see is president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, and the only other name that we see is General Anton Tus. This is all we know about your meeting with General Tus. You say that there were a number of such meetings. Did you perhaps try at one of those to get an answer to the following question? What was the military objective that Croatia wanted to achieve by laying siege to all the JNA barracks throughout Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned to you a few moments ago, the Croatian side had relatively few weapons at this time. I would say the proportion was 90 to 10, if you ask me to put a number on it, as compared with the JNA which, of course, was a large army, in 1991, the eighth largest army in Europe. The Croatians, as I reported, felt that by blockading the barracks they would have, so to speak, a quid for the quo, when it came to talking about their independence and JNA withdrawal from the country. So I think that was what probably the Croatians had in mind by blockading the JNA barracks in the country. It was somewhat of a desperate act, I think, on the part of the underdogs because they were so heavily outgunned, I mean, in terms of the destruction being wrought in the country we reported on that. May I tell you what the decision was about this point? May I inform the Court? It might be useful. If you want to know our view at the time. I can tell you, if you wish. But it's up to you. I think the Court might find it useful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this matter, I would like to show you a document. Before that, however, I will have to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to show the witness a document. We do have a problem in this regard, however, which I would like to deal with, with your assistance. The document that I wish to show the witness and subsequently tender into evidence is one of the 65 ter -- Rule 65 ter list documents, one of the documents placed by the OTP on their list. All these were filed confidentially, although not all of the individual portions are confidential, especially not the list as such. I would like to ask this. The document is marked as a Rule 70 document. First of all, I would like to have this document shown to the Trial Chamber, through E-Court, and to the OTP as well. I move that this document not be shown outside this courtroom or to the witness for the time being. In these situations, when one of the parties wishes to show a Rule 70 document, are we required to go into private session or not? Therefore, with your permission, I will ask for this document to be displayed on the screen in the courtroom but not outside, and the number is R0320966. It's a three-page document. If this doesn't work, in that case, Your Honours, I have copies. Your Honours, I believe I said this. Just to be on the safe side, I don't think the witness should be shown this document for the time being, and then it will be up to the Chamber to decide whether or not the witness will eventually be shown this document. Your Honours, I hear from my colleagues that the image is not very clear, the one that we have on our screens. I have prepared printed copies of this document, and I would like to ask the usher to get the copies from me and distribute them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. While that is occurring, Mr. Moore, have you any submission on whether this document needs to remain in confidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know exactly what the document was. I haven't had an opportunity of perusing it. I know it's come from OTP but we have no notice of what is arriving in cross-examination. May I be permitted a few moments to look at the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed. I thought you may have looked at it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. We had not received notice of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, while my learned friend is looking at that document, I would like to share something about the document with you. Although this is a Rule 70 document, it is quite clear that the substance of this document has already been shown in a public place with no restrictions. This is about someone who was mentioned today on the cross-examination. This person presented a position which was subsequently published by the media. Regardless, the document bears this mark or is marked as a Rule 70 document which prompts me to address you on this matter. Alternatively, Your Honour, we should have a break in five minutes, so maybe if we break five minutes early so that Mr. Moore may have an opportunity to go through the document and the Chamber can then decide on the status of this document that I would like to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that will be a practical course. We will use the break to enable Mr. Moore to form a view. Are there questions you want to put now or would you like to break now? We will have a slightly early break --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm allowed, once I have asked questions about this document, having received permission from the Chamber, I will have an additional five to ten questions to ask the witness after the break. Therefore, I think it might be a better idea to have the break now. That's if you agree, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will resume -- Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All I'm asking is if there are any other documents of this nature, if they can be shown to us now, it will stop applications for adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I thank the Court for the time. We are in agreement for this to go before the witness. It can go in the open court format. Can I just indicate, so it assists, at least I hope it assists, in actual fact it is a news article from Novi Vjesnik and clearly is a reported speech on what has been given by way of lecture. If it's to be used as a principle for reported speech in an article that is relative to the issues before the Court, we would support that course of conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. If the document could come on to the witness's and the public screens. Thank you. Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to give the witness some time to go through the document so that he may familiarise himself with the substance of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say you had a paper copy of it? Not -- if you had one, I'm sure the witness would find it much easier to read. You've only got yours? That's all right. We'll just have to persist with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in fact, I have several copies, and I think it's a good idea to let the witness have a printed copy, a hard copy. I prepared copies because I didn't know whether the copies on the screen would be legible. They tend to be quite blurred sometimes. If the usher could please distribute these copies. And with your permission, Your Honour, I will ask the witness to yet again identify whether the image displayed on the screen is identical to what the witness has in front of him. In order to be as brief as possible, I have taken the liberty to highlight some of the passages in yellow to facilitate the witness's progress through this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you say you had any spare for the members of the Court? We are very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for assisting me, Your Honour. While the document is being distributed, I would like to say that we only have this document in English. The OTP has not yet had this document translated. The Defence teams are making an effort to have their documents translated and we believe that priority should be given to those that are originally in B/C/S, so that we can avoid situations where the witness is unable to analyse the document. Since this witness speaks English, we treat this document as an original and the witness should not have a difficult time commenting on the document. I also move that the document be marked for identification until such time as I'm able to have an official translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I will ask you two or three questions in relation to this document. If you look at the highlighted portions well, that's what I'm interested in. You say that you met General Tus and that you talked to him on several occasions. As you can see, this was a public lecture given by General Tus. The media published this lecture in February 1993. The date is not readily legible on the face of the document. When you arrived in the former Yugoslavia, as you confirmed before the break -- I mean about what happened in relation to the barracks -- was it not clear that the Croatian authorities were laying siege to the barracks in order to obtain the weapons that were in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was clear to us in some barracks. In others, they never got the weapons. For example, or at least they didn't get all of them certainly, because when we were in Osijek, we could see the JNA barracks, and the JNA troops in Osijek, in fact, fired tank fire, we were informed, heavy tank guns, into the populace of Osijek, and the city underwent some shelling; not a great deal but some. So that was one case. In other cases, I have no doubt that the Croatians got weapons from the JNA. As I mentioned earlier, they essentially started out with no army and very few weapons, so it's understandable that they would seek weapons and it varied quite a lot from barracks to barracks. During our lengthy visit to the Marshal Tito caserne in Zagreb, which I reported on extensively, four pages long, just the description of the meeting in my diary notes, General Raseta informed us during that meeting that one of the Croatian conditions that were put to him in connection with the unblocking of the barracks was that the JNA leave its weapons behind and he refused that condition. So the short answer is yes, they tried to get weapons from the barracks. I don't find that surprising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. If you turn the next page, marked as 0968, the four last digits, it seems that pagination is not quite clear. It's just how this was published. The second page on your screen. Let me just see these figures. No. That doesn't seem right. Could we have the previous page, please, on the screen? Yes. That's the right page. My apologies to you, Mr. Okun. We have technical issues here. What you see on the screen now is something that we are interested in. There is a paragraph beginning with the words: "In that way we captured" and so on. Can you find that in the text?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Line 5 and 6 reads: "And much of this was sent to Vukovar and other crisis areas." You as observers on a mission entrusted to you by the United Nations, was it clear to you that the weapons thus obtained, namely by blocking the JNA barracks, were being sent to Vukovar and other crisis areas?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did not go into the provenance of each and every weapon. Nobody would expect us to do that. We did observe the weapons. I've already reported that we saw the Serb gunners surrounding Vukovar as we drove into the city. We saw them in the field, in the town. We -- I've reported to you that, it's in my diary notes that you have, that we saw destroyed tanks in the streets of Vukovar. So, of course, we were aware that a war was going on. And you can't have a war without weapons. And it was also very obvious that the overwhelming superiority in the matter of armament rested with the JNA, since it was the -- or had been the formerly constituted army of a country. That didn't surprise us either. What was, however, shocking was the disproportionate use of force that was being applied, and we reported that to the Security Council and to General Kadijevic and to Milosevic at the time. We've gone over that yesterday. I don't think there is any need to repeat it. I can, if you wish. But, of course, we were aware that there were weapons and that 90 per cent, or something like 90 per cent of the fire-power, I would guess 90 per cent, was in the hands and under the control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until what time?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation altered, of course, over time. The -- several things happened to the JNA, which we are all aware of. It's a matter of common knowledge that the JNA was -- became smaller in size, both for unofficial reasons, one might put it, as the members of the JNA from the republics that had declared independence, many of them left the JNA to return to their home countries. General Tus was an example. He had been a senior officer of the JNA before going back to Croatia. So that was one thing. The other thing that affected the JNA was the desertion rate of the enlisted men and the fact that many of the call-ups were not fully answered. So that over time, the JNA very quickly became a Serbian army, not a Yugoslav army. This was reported to us by the prime minister of Yugoslavia, by Mr. Markovic. You will find it in my diary recorded that from Prime Minister Ante Markovic telling Mr. Vance and me that the JNA has become Serbised, Serbised were his very words. So that is one of the continuing factors, both the reduction in size of the JNA, which happened mostly in 1992, but beginning with the declarations of independence of the four republics, Slovenia, Bosnia, Croatia and Macedonia. They lost a lot of men from those republics. And that was the factual situation of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun.
