And my last question pertaining to this document: Were you and Mr. Vance aware, either by having direct knowledge of the situation or through reports you received from the ground, that the population of Slavonia had problems in leaving the areas engulfed by war?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were made aware via numerous sources that there were movements of both of the nationalities, more than both, there were some Hungarians in the areas, some Czechs, and because of the fighting in Eastern Slavonia -- am I correct in assuming that when you say Slavonia, you mean Eastern Slavonia, not Western Slavonia? The situation was different in Western Slavonia. But in Eastern Slavonia where there is in many opstinas no majority population, there was great movement, and as I've already reported to the Court, we visited one of the refugee camps where we witnessed affecting scenes and women weeping. They were Croatians, however. And we also were told of a refugee inflow into Serbia from that area. We were informed of that situation. And, of course, we made the logical assumption, which I think was correct, that the people leaving Eastern Slavonia and going into Serbia itself were Serbs. So there was a large-scale displacement of persons. But if we look at the bottom line, as they now say in America, namely if we sum it all up, the overwhelming number of refugees were Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like now to put a specific question about a paragraph in this document based on which we can see -- or rather, would you agree with my interpretation of the words of General Tus, that it was the Croatian interest to keep the residents in the cities of Eastern Slavonia? Would you interpret this sentence in this way?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, which sentence are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise if I failed to direct you, Mr. Okun. It's the same page, third paragraph from the bottom, last sentence, which begins: "The basic thing for us General Tus said" --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I've found it now. Thank you very much. "One of the big mistakes of the Yugo army concept" - I'm reading it aloud myself - "was in not going further in their penetration and capture in the surrounded cities later. They wanted instead to first clear the entire territory captured and destroy everything that was Croatian. The basic thing General Tus said, was to keep the people in the cities of Eastern Slavonia." Well, I find that consistent. I don't think you would want to denude your territory. To do so would be to give de facto control to whoever -- whoever occupied it. It's important to bear in mind that for whatever reason the JNA chose at this time not to storm the cities, that is, the infantry didn't charge into the cities, which I think they probably could have done with armour support. Instead, they shelled them very heavily from outside. The pattern was the same in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We all know about the shelling of Sarajevo. This was a matter of concern, but also many of the western military observers wondered at the JNA tactic, and it is still a matter, I suppose, of debate in military circles. But the answer to your question regarding General Tus's comment to try and not denude the Croatian cities in Eastern Slavonia of their Croatian people, I don't find that surprising. I think that's a normal reaction. As you know, during the battle of Stalingrad, the people of Stalingrad lived in the city. They were in shell holes but they lived in the city. There is a monument to the people of Stalingrad precisely for that reason. You can see it if you visit the city which is now called Vulgograd. I have seen it. So I don't think it is a surprising thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unfortunately I must say that I cannot agree with you concerning this comparison between Vukovar and Stalingrad, because we are now dealing with the desire of the Croatian government to keep the citizens in the towns of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I have no further questions concerning this document and I now tender it into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would ask that that be marked for identification because, as I say, it's a report from a newspaper. If, however, as a general principle, such a document as this, namely a newspaper or reported speech is to be admitted by way as an exhibit, then as a general principle, then, of course, I'll agree to that. But it must be one principal to apply to all documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, this document will be marked for identification, as you request, until such time as you've had an opportunity to verify the source, being one of your discovered documents. That shouldn't, I would expect, be a major problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, not at all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this will be document marked for identification number 71.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have just one more question for you, Mr. Okun. Yesterday, in several instances you mentioned the existence of paramilitary formations in the territory of Croatia. You also mentioned your observations about them. You mentioned Slivovitz and you mentioned Paraga. Since this is my last question, I would like to ask you to explain to me whether at the time you knew about the convicts' battalion as a special purpose formation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Madam, on whose side was the convicts' battalion fighting?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a Croatian paramilitary formation.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't believe I was made aware of that. It's possible, but I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about turbo Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard frequent references to Ustasha. It was the standard Serb appellation for the Croatians, and any Croatian in uniform was regularly called Ustasha. So we heard a lot about Ustasha, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question pertained to turbo Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Turbo, I don't recall any specific references to turbo Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question is: Did you hear of the 204th Vukovar Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Tapuskovic. Mr. Lukic? Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Okun. My name is Novak Lukic. I am an attorney-at-law from Belgrade, and in this trial I'm one of two counsel representing Mr. Sljivancanin. I'm by myself today. I will now be putting questions to you, and you probably have already guessed that the line of my questioning will be somewhat different from the questions put to you by my colleagues and that I will mostly focus on the topics you discussed during examination-in-chief, and the reasons for that are probably clear to you. Now I would like to put several questions to you regarding your diaries. I would like first to sum up, to see whether I understood well the process of keeping diaries, based on your yesterday's and today's answers. I understood it that you entered information into your diaries on a daily basis immediately during the day or shortly thereafter, after the event that you wanted to record in your diaries. I took it that when you toured Yugoslavia, you wrote your diaries every day, in hotels and, as you said yesterday, while driving in a car en route to somewhere else. Did I understand this well? I'm especially interested in the pace of data recording.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have it right, Mr. Lukic. Quite right. The diaries -- I wrote them not at the end of the day but at the time the event was occurring. That's to say, if I'm at a meeting, take the meeting with General Raseta in the Tito caserne. We are there for an hour and a half. He makes a presentation. Colonel Djurovski makes a presentation. I record that as they are talking. Summarising it, as I said yesterday. I'm not a court stenographer but I summarised the important points. I know what their points are. I know what we are listening to hear. I know what they are trying to say. I would note anything that, you know, that might be surprising, that sort of thing, and when I heard something important, I put it in quotations. Now, that happened at the time, at meetings seated around the table with General Kadijevic, with Milosevic, with Gligorov, with Izetbegovic, all of them. But there were times when we were more active. For example, in Vukovar we were getting in and out of the armoured personnel carriers, and there, I would probably wait 15 minutes or so, and inside the carrier write it. But on no occasion did I wait even to the end of the day because there were simply too many meetings, as you could see by my diaries. The diaries, incidentally, which cover the entire period of my activity in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, run to almost 2.000 pages. And they were mostly written, you know, at the time we were seeing things. So the -- or they were summaries. You'll see sometimes in the diary, let us say I had dinner with Mr. Vance and Mr. Milosevic and Jovanovic. That happened more than once. Well, as a guest, I wasn't going to take out my notebook over the caviar and the meat course. I didn't think that would be polite. I don't think anybody would do that as a guest of the president of Serbia. But immediately on repairing to the hotel, right at the end of the meeting, I would note and so note in the diary that it was a summary of the meeting, to make very clear for the record that it was not word-for-word, that it was summarising the meeting. So having done this for many years and being very experienced at it, I continued to do it during the Yugoslav missions because of the fact that they were so intense, and it was necessary to recall what we were hearing and seeing in order to report back to the Security Council, which was our task. And as I informed Madam Tapuskovic, the previous counsel, we reported regularly, orally and in writing, after every mission. I hope that makes it clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, now, with your answer, you have in fact reminded me that you testified extensively about this in the Milosevic trial. I think it is also useful for us to hear that in this courtroom, in this trial. I'm mostly interested in the Vukovar events but you gave this explanation and it will be of great assistance.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I make a very brief point? You will see if you read the transcripts of the Milosevic trial, which you just mentioned, that on numerous occasions, Mr. Milosevic, who had all of the diaries, referred to them in cross-examining me, which of course was his perfect right to do so. I should add that at no time did he ever, by word or even by hint or suggestion, at no time did he ever challenge the accuracy and the veracity of the diaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now that we are dealing with the diary, I will now have to revisit the issue that has to do with the fact that we received only several pages of your diary but not more than that. Initially, that didn't seem as a problem, but now it emerges that perhaps it would have been useful for us to receive the diaries in the entirety, especially since the public and the Prosecution have had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, no, I'm sorry, there have been repeated complaint about this. There has been not a single request from the Defence at any time for any other pages, apart from the ones that we supplied. I've had this checked to clarify. If my learned friend knows of some document that anyone has sent to the Prosecution, I will clearly withdraw that, but we received not a single request for anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what prompted this reaction of my learned friend. All I wanted was to clarify with the witness the fact that we could have perhaps taken advantage of the entire diary. Based on the events recorded in the diary, it seems that there is a discrepancy between the number of pages and the brevity of the time that elapsed between various events. Therefore, it might be something that the Trial Chamber would like to hear about, to explain this discrepancy between the number of pages and the passage of time, a very brief passage of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not the concern at the moment of the Chamber, Mr. Lukic. If you have a point to make about it with the witness, he has the diaries there. Pursue it, if you want to know what happened or what is noted on the pages between the pages you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's precisely that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, you have your diaries in front of you. We do not have all of the pages. On your page 39 that you gave evidence about yesterday, and that is the page dealing with the 18th of November, when you had meetings with UNHCR and ICRC people and mentioned the term "mushroom people." So the events of the 18th. In your diary, that's on page 39, and that's a page that we received. Then following that, we learn the events recorded on page 63, which is actually the next day, the following day. So can you please explain to us what happened between these pages? What happened and what was recorded in these 30 pages when we are dealing with just a 24 period of time, 24-hour period of time, but it seems to take quite a lot of pages in your diary, and would that be something that would be of interest to us?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm happy to do so, if -- no problem. First, might I mention a clarification, Mr. Lukic? You mentioned in a previous question that the diaries had been made public, that they were available to the public. That is not the case. They have never, at no time, been available to the public. They have been under either my personal possession or, for the last three years, they have been physically under the control of the Registrar of this Tribunal. Now, what happened? All right. I'll just give you the sequence that you've asked for. It's quite simple. It's in the diary. November 18, 1991, Monday, at 8.15, Mr. Vance and I discuss our work programme and logistics. We meet from 10.00 to 10.50 with the UNHCR and the ICRC. This is in Belgrade. From 11.10 a.m. until 1.55 p.m., in Belgrade that day, the 18th, we meet with President Milosevic and Foreign Minister Jovanovic. From 12.30 p.m. to 1.55 p.m., Mr. Vance and I have lunch with Milosevic and Jovanovic. That's page 49. And as I reported to you earlier, since I didn't want to take notes during the caviar, I wrote a summary of that meeting. I'll be happy to read it now if you wish to hear it. But to continue on what happened on -- I'm continuing from that. We went immediately to General Kadijevic and met from 2 p.m. to 3.30 p.m. with General Kadijevic, Admiral Brovet and Colonel Vuk Obradovic. We are still on the 18th and we are still in Belgrade. I continue. We left that meeting in mid-afternoon and went back to the hotel for Mr. Vance to rest. And then at 8.00 on the 18th, 8.00 p.m. to 9.15 p.m., we met with the prime minister of Yugoslavia, Prime Minister Ante Markovic, and his undersecretary from the foreign ministry, Mr. Veres. I've already reported on that meeting in answer to questions. It was at that meeting, for example, that he said the -- that Bosnia-Herzegovina was a potential atomic -- atom bomb. That was the 18th. And that takes us to page 60. At page 61, you have, and it begins in Belgrade with our departure, our -- well, our wake-up at 5.00 a.m. and our departure at 6.30, courtesy of the JNA, for Vukovar. So that gives you the entire picture of what happened between pages 39 and page 61.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for what I said about the public nature of the diaries. I knew, based on the transcript, that the diaries were only given to the OTP. That's one thing I wanted to say. On the other hand, based on what you just said, I understand that due to the nature of your business there, which was to compile a report for the Security Council, you decided to prioritise, in terms of diary space, the events that you believed were particularly important. And then it goes page by page. This is something that I now fully understand. Now for a brief question. Based on your notes from the meeting with the representatives of the UNHCR and the ICRC, this concept, the mushroom people, where does this concept come from? Is this something you heard from somebody, or is it a mental image or a metaphor that you used for your purposes at the time? Can you please clarify this?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's very easy to clarify. I put it in quotes. It was used by the ICRC representative as he was talking about the civilians who were trapped underground by the shelling of the city. That's what he meant by mushroom people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is in relation to that. You appear to have had regular contacts with the ICRC, the UNHCR and the ECMM. I would like to know this: The information that you obtained from the International Red Cross in relation to what the JNA did, to the actions of the JNA, how would you characterise the information that they gave you? Was it only critical or were there positive things that they said about the JNA too?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICRC, and I may say the UNHCR and other people but specifically to your question about the ICRC, was very broad-ranging, very, very fair. The ICRC, as we all know, as an organisation, one of its key principles is neutrality and impartiality and independence. Those three are perhaps the three key principles on which the organisation has worked for more than 100 years. And they continue to work that way. And the ICRC people - and we met more than one, of course - I always found extremely careful and very balanced in their analysis and appreciation of the factual situation. I thought they were quite, quite good, and quite fair-minded. Where they had to apportion blame, they apportioned blame. Where they found reason to praise, they had no hesitancy in praising, as Mr. Vance and I had no reluctance to hear that. Remember, we were there also as impartial fact-finders. Our task, which Mr. Vance insisted on and I did it at all times, was to be honest mediators between the sides. And I think, if I may say, I think the Court can see that in the way Mr. Vance was received, in the way that both sides asked us to assist when General Kadijevic told us that blocking, blockading the barracks was a major problem, we made that our principal task, certainly very high on the list, to unblock those barracks. That is to say, to get the Croatian government to unblock the barricades. And I've already reported yesterday that I was given the charge specifically of remaining in Yugoslavia after Mr. Vance returned to work on the problem of unblocking the barricades. So we took it very seriously. And I think the ICRC took its humanitarian role very seriously. I never had any indication to the contrary that the ICRC was partial, from what I could observe. Now, I wasn't obviously everywhere all the time. Nobody can be. But I think they lived up to their impartiality and neutrality requirement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 19th of November, in Vukovar, you personally saw representatives of the International Red Cross? This note, the diary, page 63, I see that Mr. Vance refers to an active presence, as he says, of the International Red Cross. Is this something that rings a bell, namely that you saw one of their representatives or even talked to them in the area? And then my next question, if you don't mind, do you remember if the fact was mentioned on that occasion that a large number of Croatian soldiers had surrendered on the previous day who were taken to the Sremska Mitrovica prison and that the ICRC was involved to a great extent? And as a result, that everybody was happy with this operation? Is this something that rings a bell?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't. I don't recall meeting or seeing any ICRC representative on November 19. It's possible because you know we went in an open motorcade. There were many cars behind us. As I say, we were taken to Vukovar by the JNA. You know, we stopped at Sid, et cetera. We moved on. Many, many journalists were there. I've already reported that. You've seen it on the video. We have all been aware of that. So I would not exclude the possibility that there were other people there, but I personally have no knowledge. On your second question, about the capture of Croatians and their being taken to a prison, I don't believe that was raised. Our prime interest was in first seeing the area and then visiting the hospital. And the barracks, which we did see the barracks but we never saw the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked this question because on page 63 of your diary, it reads: "Cyrus Vance visited Vukovar today. Tragedy, a serious humanitarian problem. International Red Cross active." My understanding was that you had direct information or that you personally saw this. Or is this something that Mr. Vance had heard from someone and then conveyed to the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the day before, we had met the ICRC representative, as you pointed out and we discussed, so we knew of their activity. It did not mean we were in personal contact with them on the 19th, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have already mentioned President Tudjman. I will ask something in relation to one of the questions that Mrs. Tapuskovic, my colleague, asked you towards the end of her cross-examination. It will be a rather direct question, maybe not so direct, but, well, you spoke about civilians in cities and in relation to that document you know. In any one of your talks with President Tudjman and the Croatian leaders, were you ever told about the position of the Croatian leadership that for them the fact of civilians leaving their towns would have constituted an act of ethnic cleansing? Are you familiar with this political angle to this problem?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were of course aware of the population displacement. I've discussed that frequently. There have been numerous questions on it. I've answered them. Just to recall one facet, in our first report to the Security Council, at the end of October 1991, after the first mission, we already had a separate annex. You may read it. It's a public document. A separate annex on the humanitarian situation. That is to say, the refugee problem. So we were well aware of it. Mr. Vance and I took the humanitarian situation on both sides into deep account. Did Tudjman refer to this? Of course, he did. He naturally referred to it from his point of view and would talk about Serb and/or JNA depredations, just as Mr. Milosevic would report to us from his point of view about the evil activities being carried out by the Croatians. I think I've already mentioned and it's noted in my diary notes, that he told us that one Croatian soldier was wearing a necklace that was made up of the fingers of Serb children that had been cut off. But we never saw that person and, of course, he never produced the person. But those kinds of allegations, some of which I'm sure were exaggerated and some of which I'm sure were true, were frequently made by both sides. And as impartial arbitrators, as honest go-betweens, it was our task to judge the statements on the basis of the reality that we saw or that we heard and checked. Again, this is I think what one would say normal procedure. We were, for example, aware, although we did not visit Western Slavonia, we were made aware and were aware that many Serb civilians had been driven out of Western Slavonia, places like Daruvar, Pakrac, you know them better than I, and were in Bosnia-Herzegovina, south of the Sava River. That had been made clear to us. And that sort of thing was constant, that the -- the large-scale movement of peoples, voluntary and involuntary, which normally occurs in war. With specific reference to the term "ethnic cleansing," that was not used to the best of my knowledge during the conflict in Croatia. That became a term that was more popularly used during the fighting in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we've run more than an hour now. We must have another break. And we'll resume at half past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe my next two questions will allow for brief answers. Did you at any point in time during your missions hear from anyone you talked to, the Serbian leadership, the Croatian leadership, the Croatian army, that the Croatian side also shelled some areas of the town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard about Croatian shelling in other places, and in Bosnia there were allegations of shelling, but that's not at issue here, but I don't recall anybody telling us about Croatian shelling at Vukovar. It's possible, but I don't recall it. I would have to really consult the diaries for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've spoken a lot about the blockade of the barracks. I see that you have a lot of information on that. Does the Varazdin barracks ring a bell and the Varazdin Corps? Do you know anything about that, that you could perhaps share with us, about the blockade of that particular barracks?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems I won't be asking you any further questions about that, then. I will now move to a different subject. But just one question, something in relation to one of the questions asked by my colleague, Ms. Tapuskovic. As far as I understand, you never provided a written statement to the OTP concerning your visit to Vukovar, only the one that was in relation to Mr. Slobodan Milosevic, the one that we have seen. Please allow me to clarify. We only received the transcripts of your testimonies in the Milosevic and Krajisnik cases. Did the OTP ever ask you to provide a written statement about your experience during your visit to Vukovar? A written statement to the OTP, a very brief question.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to the best of my knowledge. Am I correct in assuming that OTP stands for the Office of the Prosecutor? Yes. So that is the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like to move on to specific events, and what I will call the timing of your visit to Vukovar. I will not now be showing you a map of Vukovar. I believe we shall have other witnesses who will indicate certain locations for us. But as far as I understood your testimony in chief, and based on the video clips that we have seen, as well as some of your notes, would I be right in stating that you were aware of the existence of Operations Group North and Operations Group South in the Vukovar theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were made aware of that at some point during our visit that day. We were not made aware of it before the day. As I noted in the diary, at the bottom of page 61, if you could draw your attention to the next-to-last line. I note half hour briefing by JNA colonel, commander of southern front. So it obviously was mentioned to us as he was introduced to us, and at one point in the altercation between Mr. Vance and Major Sljivancanin, and I've been made aware of that and heard it at the time, the question was raised of northern command versus southern command. So it was during the visit at about that time during the altercation that we were made aware of that distinction. I apologise if my answers seem longer to you than they should. I realise the need to move on, but it is not possible usually to answer very briefly, and I try to be of assistance and answer fully. I have sworn to tell not just the truth but the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember whether during your visit to Negoslavci you were shown the lines of delimitation between these two operations groups? Please confirm if you do.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, and I rather doubt that we were shown it, but it's possible that during the briefing we were shown that. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go first after you left Negoslavci? This is your visit to Vukovar. Do you remember what was the first building that you came across based on your notes and on your recollection? Could you specify the time when you reached the first location in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We reached Vukovar at 11.00 a.m., 11.00 in the morning. As I noticed, the day was sunny and cloudy with -- mixed sun and clouds, no rain. We drove through the city coming into it from the south. Negoslavci lies to the south, as you know. And we may have made some stops en route, very brief ones, to look at this or that destroyed building. But the building we saw first, we were taken to -- the major thing that we saw first was the JNA barracks. Then the reception centre, then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take one step at a time, please. When I look at page 62 in your diaries, I see that you arrived in Vukovar at 11.00 and left Vukovar at 3.00 p.m. presumably. This is mentioned twice. My conclusion is that you left Vukovar at around 1300 hours in an APC and that you arrived in Belgrade at around 1430 hundred hours. I said 1300 hours. It was from 1100 to 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It's so noted in my diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said yesterday that you found out about my client's name later on. Based on your recollection, sir, when did you first hear the full name, or only the family name perhaps, of my present client, Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I only know -- learned his Christian name, his first name, when I was called to testify here. I learned his family name, as I say, sometime after the incident. I did not know it at the time. Probably within a month or so. I mean very shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was that Mr. Vance for the first time expressed his desire to visit the hospital? Was it before you left Belgrade? Was it when you arrived in Negoslavci? Or was it when you arrived in Vukovar? When was the first time you officially expressed this desire to someone on the JNA side?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You informed some of the military authorities that you were in touch related to the task of organising your visit?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As we've already established that the visit to the hospital to look into the humanitarian situation, there was the prime reason for the visit. So naturally, Mr. Vance, as a matter of routine, as a matter of organisation, as a matter of courtesy, was going to tell our JNA hosts the purpose of our visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We saw that video clip yesterday. It has been tendered today. Do you remember, in relation to my client, whether that was the first time your desire to mention -- to visit the hospital was mentioned during your dialogue? And when did this conversation take place? We have three locations in actual fact. We have the barracks, we have your visit to the refugee centre called Velepromet, everyone in this courtroom knows that, and after that you're going to the hospital. This dialogue that we saw on the video clip yesterday, can you please provide a specific time line when this dialogue took place?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several dialogues, more than one. We would be in the APCs, drive for a bit, get out. Mr. Vance expressed a desire to go to the hospital. He was told, well, we have to get back in. We would go in and out and in and out. So there were -- it was a running dialogue. The dialogue was running. Mr. Vance wasn't running. The major wasn't running. The dialogue was a running dialogue which got increasingly unpleasant as time wore on. I would say the high point, or perhaps we should call it the low point, of the exchange occurred probably about 12.40 or 12.45 a.m., because after it was made abundantly clear that force would be used to prevent us from getting to the hospital, at that point naturally we had to get back into the APCs and go to Belgrade. So it would probably have been certainly between 12.30 and 1.00 p.m., or as you say 1300 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you analysed the video clip that we saw that was on page 24 of the draft transcript, line 23. And you said: "You could see the look of anger [In English] and sternness on Cyrus Vance's face because he had said it several times already." [Interpretation] Maybe I'm asking too much now, but I'm interested in the dialogue that we saw on the footage. Do you remember whether prior to that, the request to tour the hospital was mentioned by Mr. Vance to my client? Can you remember whether that's the case?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember. As I said repeatedly, and it was known that the chief purpose of our visit was to visit the hospital. That was known from the minute we entered Vukovar. I should say more accurately it was known from the minute we departed Belgrade. That was the purpose of the -- the principal purpose of the visit, in addition to seeing the general situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I can conclude, based on your answers, that you made it abundantly clear to the organisers or to those who escorted you from Belgrade that you wanted to tour the Vukovar Hospital. Your hosts were made aware of this and very clearly too. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, not very long. It's not a very large barracks, and we walked through it. I don't suppose we were at the barracks for more than 10 or 15 minutes. Long enough to have a walk through. Since it was undamaged, there was really nothing to inspect. You always spend more time in a building, in a situation like that, if there is damage that you need to inspect or the location of the damage, the extent of the damage, that sort of thing. But when it's relatively untouched, no damage, you can just walk through it, see that, and you go on your way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The refugee centre is something that we also saw on the footage. How long did your delegation stay there? And do you remember whether there, once again, you expressed the desire to tour the hospital?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spent quite a bit of time at the refugee centre. We spoke with them. We spoke with some of the troops or -- as I said, Mr. Vance was approached by people. They -- you know, weeping, women, children in ragged clothing. It was a very, very powerful and very tragic scene. I noted that down. With regard to the hospital, again, we didn't feel we had to mention it every five minutes, but it certainly was known that it was on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Mr. Vance or any other members of the delegation, in addition to my client, spoke to any other senior officials who were present there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, and I am pretty sure of it, I wouldn't say 100 per cent but I would give it about 90 per cent, Mr. Vance spoke about the hospital exclusively to your client, or very large -- almost completely with Major Sljivancanin. As I said, they maintained a running dialogue because Major Sljivancanin, it was clear to us, was our escort officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also described to us your visit to what you termed the little hospital in Negoslavci. How long did you stay there? Did you learn what type of patients were hospitalised there?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't remain there very long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that it was said that the patients there were both Serbs and Croats as well as members of the JNA and ZNG? Did your hosts tell you anything about that?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that was mentioned to us, that there was a mixed patient population in that small hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is based on the information I received from my client and it has to do with the dialogue with Mr. Vance. I'm interested in knowing whether you remember this and whether you were able to hear this. Mr. Sljivancanin claims that at one point Mr. Vance asked him whether the JNA intended to proceed further towards Osijek, and when Sljivancanin said that the JNA had no intention of going anywhere but that it was rather carrying out its constitutional duties, Mr. Vance told him then that in Osijek, 80 per cent of the population considered the JNA to be an aggressor's army. Do you remember any such conversation that had to do with Osijek?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that specific conversation. As I've said, Mr. Vance and Major Sljivancanin were having an intermittent but continuous dialogue on a variety of issues as we thought we were being taken to the hospital that we had asked to see, and that the interchanges between Mr. Vance and Major Sljivancanin became increasingly acrimonious. That was clear to all. You could see it on the video as well. Indeed, as I've already testified, I've known Mr. Vance for many decades, I had never seen him as exercised or as angry as he was that morning in -- at the treatment he was receiving at the hands of Major Sljivancanin. I might add to that, Mr. Lukic, since you mention Osijek, that it would have been logical for Mr. Vance to mention Osijek in Vukovar because Osijek is larger, it's the capital city, it's nearby, and we had already -- also heard reports about the attacks on Osijek and visited Osijek just 10 days later. We had the same kind of visit to Osijek that we did in Vukovar. It was handled somewhat differently because the front line was outside the city. We had to be handed over from the JNA to the Croatian army. Incidents occurred on the road. I don't need to go into them here. But in any case, it was logical for Mr. Vance to mention Osijek since we knew about it. It was not a hostile question. Rather, it was a question for information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a correction for the transcript. Page 67, line 25, my question was that 80 per cent of the population of Osijek were Croats. That is not reflected in the transcript. Do you remember that during that visit, you were taken to an elevation in that area called Milovo Brdo from where one can see the panorama of the city, including the hospital, as my client claims, and that Mr. Vance was even given binoculars to look at the city. Do you remember being taken to this elevation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT STUART OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we can skip three minutes of today's trial, it I think would be wise because I'm about to begin with another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now and will resume in the morning at 10.00. That seems to be all in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: be reconvened on Friday, the 18th day of November, 2005, at 10.00 a.m. 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m., to
